tagline: Sahara sands and the great river
overview:
Niger is a landlocked country in West Africa, roughly twice the size of Texas and mostly Sahara Desert. Its name comes from the Niger River, which curves through the far southwestern corner and supplies the country's only major waterway, its capital, and much of its best farmland. Algeria and Libya lie to the north, with Chad, Nigeria, Benin, Burkina Faso, and Mali around the other sides.

About 26 million people live in Niger, nearly all of them in the greener southern strip near the Nigerian border. French is the official language, while Hausa, Zarma, Tamasheq, Fulfulde, and Kanuri are the languages of daily life. Niamey, the capital, stands on the banks of the Niger River.

Niger has one of the youngest populations on Earth, with about half its people under fifteen. Most families grow millet and sorghum or herd cattle, goats, and camels, and uranium is mined in the desert north. Niger is a republic, though the army seized power in a coup in 2023.
landAndNature: Most of Niger is desert. The Ténéré, a sea of sand and gravel in the east, is one of the emptiest places on the planet, and the dark volcanic Aïr Mountains rise from it, hiding pools and rock paintings made by herders back when the Sahara was green. Daytime temperatures often pass 40 degrees Celsius. In the south a belt of dry grassland called the Sahel gets a short rainy season, and the Niger River floods each year, watering rice fields where hippos wallow. The last wild giraffes in West Africa, a pale subspecies, wander among villages near Kouré, and W National Park shelters elephants, lions, and cheetahs.
peopleAndCulture: Niger's largest groups are the Hausa and Zarma farmers of the south, with Tuareg, Fulani, Kanuri, and Toubou herders across the north. Nearly everyone is Muslim. Millet is the staple, pounded into flour for thick porridge or dumplings and eaten with sauces of baobab leaf, okra, or peanut. Tuareg men wear the tagelmust, a long indigo head cloth, and travel by camel; the silver Agadez cross they make is worn all across West Africa. At the Cure Salée gathering, Wodaabe men dance the Gerewol for hours in bright makeup while women judge them. Traditional wrestling is the national sport, with a yearly championship that fills stadiums.
history: Rock art in the Sahara shows people herding cattle and hunting here thousands of years ago, when the desert was grassland. Later the region sat astride trans-Saharan caravan routes; Agadez grew into a major trading city, and parts of Niger came under the Songhai, Bornu, and Hausa states. France conquered the territory around 1900 and governed it as part of French West Africa. Niger became independent on August 3, 1960. Uranium discovered in the north brought income but also dependence on world prices, severe droughts struck in the 1970s and 1980s, and Tuareg rebellions broke out in the desert. Elected governments and military coups have alternated since, most recently in 2023.
funFacts: Niger and neighboring Nigeria are both named after the Niger River, which crosses only one corner of Niger itself.
The Tree of Ténéré was once the most isolated tree on Earth, with no other tree within about 400 kilometers.
Niger holds some of Africa's richest dinosaur beds; Nigersaurus, found here, had more than 500 teeth in a wide, straight-edged mouth.
The mud-brick minaret of the Agadez mosque, about 27 meters tall and studded with wooden beams, has been rebuilt for centuries.
Roughly 600 West African giraffes, the last wild ones anywhere, live unfenced among farms southeast of Niamey.
